newsitem.title: USA: Bowles denies Hubbell got Whitewater "hush money".
newsitem.headline: Bowles denies Hubbell got Whitewater "hush money".

text.p: White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles denied on Tuesday that former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell was paid hush money to keep quiet on President Bill Clinton's role in the Whitewater scandal.
"Absolutely not," Bowles said when reporters asked whether Hubbell was paid off to stay silent. Bowles then went in to testify before a special Whitewater grand jury in Little Rock.

He received a subpoena from the grand jury on April 4 demanding both documents and testimony. Three days earlier, the White House disclosed that Bowles and former Chief of Staff Thomas "Mack" McLarty had sought to help Hubbell find work after he resigned from his Justice Department post.
"I am just going to answer the questions asked by the special prosecutor," Bowles said on Tuesday. McLarty was expected to testify before the grand jury later this week.

Hubbell, once a close friend of Clinton and a law partner of his wife Hillary Rodham Clinton, resigned as associate attorney general in 1994 amid controversy over his private law practice. Later that year he pleaded guilty to fraudulent billing of clients at the Rose Law Firm in Little Rock before he joined the Clinton administration and was jailed in 1995.

Both Bowles and McLarty made phone calls on his behalf in the months after his resignation but the White House has said they were unaware at that point of his illegal acts and rejected suggestions that the help amounted to hush money.
Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr was trying to determine whether the jobs provided to Hubbell after he left the Justice Department were intended to buy his silence.
Clinton has said he saw nothing improper about the calls and that both Bowles and McLarty were simply showing "human compassion" for a man with four children who was out of work.
Hubbell has denied withholding information that might damage the president and first lady as the Whitewater scandal has resurfaced to put the White House under renewed pressure.

James McDougal, Clinton's former partner in the failed Whitewater real estate venture that lies at the centre of the scandal, was sentenced to just three years in prison on Monday after agreeing to cooperate with Starr's investigators. He had faced up to 81 years in prison for his conviction last May on 18 counts of fraud and conspiracy.

McDougal has reportedly reversed his earlier statements and is now telling investigators that in 1986, as governor of Arkansas, Clinton pressured a banker to extend an illegal $300,000 loan to McDougal's former wife Susan McDougal.

Clinton denied the allegation under oath during the McDougals' trial last year. Susan McDougal was sentenced to two years in prison for her part in winning the fraudulent loan but, unlike her former husband, she has refused to cooperate with Starr and is serving a contempt of court sentence for refusing to testify before a grand jury.
